subtopic: Centre of Mass and its Motion
stem: Find the centre of mass of three particles at the vertices of an equilateral triangle. The masses of the particles are 100g, 150g, and 200g respectively. Each side of the equilateral triangle is 0.5m long.
solution:
With the \(x\)- and \(y\)-axes chosen as shown in Fig. 6.9, the coordinates of points O, A and B forming the equilateral triangle are respectively \((0,0)\), \((0.5,0)\), \((0.25,\,0.25\sqrt{3})\). Let the masses 100 g, 150 g and 200 g be located at O, A and B respectively. Then,

\(X = \dfrac{m_{1}x_{1} + m_{2}x_{2} + m_{3}x_{3}}{m_{1} + m_{2} + m_{3}}\)

\(= \dfrac{\left[100(0) + 150(0.5) + 200(0.25)\right]\,\text{g m}}{(100 + 150 + 200)\,\text{g}}\)

\(= \dfrac{75 + 50}{450}\,\text{m} = \dfrac{125}{450}\,\text{m} = \dfrac{5}{18}\,\text{m}\)

\(Y = \dfrac{\left[100(0) + 150(0) + 200(0.25\sqrt{3})\right]\,\text{g m}}{450\,\text{g}}\)

\(= \dfrac{50\sqrt{3}}{450}\,\text{m} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{9}\,\text{m} = \dfrac{1}{3\sqrt{3}}\,\text{m}\)

The centre of mass C is shown in the figure. Note that it is not the geometric centre of the triangle OAB. Why?

subtopic: Centre of Mass and its Motion
stem: Find the centre of mass of a triangular lamina.
solution:
The lamina \((\Delta LMN)\) may be subdivided into narrow strips each parallel to the base \((MN)\) as shown in Fig. 6.10.

By symmetry each strip has its centre of mass at its midpoint. If we join the midpoint of all the strips we get the median LP. The centre of mass of the triangle as a whole therefore, has to lie on the median LP. Similarly, we can argue that it lies on the median MQ and NR. This means the centre of mass lies on the point of concurrence of the medians, i.e. on the centroid G of the triangle.

subtopic: Centre of Mass and its Motion
stem: Find the centre of mass of a uniform L-shaped lamina (a thin flat plate) with dimensions as shown. The mass of the lamina is 3 kg.
solution:
Choosing the \(X\) and \(Y\) axes as shown in Fig. 6.11 we have the coordinates of the vertices of the L-shaped lamina as given in the figure. We can think of the L-shape to consist of 3 squares each of length 1 m. The mass of each square is 1 kg, since the lamina is uniform. The centres of mass \(C_{1}\), \(C_{2}\) and \(C_{3}\) of the squares are, by symmetry, their geometric centres and have coordinates \((1/2,\,1/2)\), \((3/2,\,1/2)\), \((1/2,\,3/2)\) respectively. We take the masses of the squares to be concentrated at these points. The centre of mass of the whole L shape \((X,\,Y)\) is the centre of mass of these mass points.

Hence

\(X = \dfrac{\left[1(1/2) + 1(3/2) + 1(1/2)\right]\,\text{kg m}}{(1 + 1 + 1)\,\text{kg}} = \dfrac{5}{6}\,\text{m}\)

\(Y = \dfrac{\left[1(1/2) + 1(1/2) + 1(3/2)\right]\,\text{kg m}}{(1 + 1 + 1)\,\text{kg}} = \dfrac{5}{6}\,\text{m}\)

The centre of mass of the L-shape lies on the line OD. We could have guessed this without calculations. Can you tell why? Suppose, the three squares that make up the L shaped lamina of Fig. 6.11 had different masses. How will you then determine the centre of mass of the lamina?

stem: Find the scalar and vector products of two vectors. \(\mathbf{a} = (3\hat{i} - 4\hat{j} + 5\hat{k})\) and \(\mathbf{b} = (-2\hat{i} + \hat{j} + 3\hat{k})\)
solution:
[Textbook misprint in the question, contradicted by its own printed solution: the stem gives \(\vec{b} = -2\hat{i} + \hat{j} + 3\hat{k}\), but every printed result in the solution below requires \(-3\hat{k}\). The scalar product \(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = -25\), the determinant row \(-2\;\;1\;\;-3\), and the cross products \(\vec{a}\times\vec{b} = 7\hat{i} - \hat{j} - 5\hat{k}\) and \(\vec{b}\times\vec{a} = -7\hat{i} + \hat{j} + 5\hat{k}\) all follow from \(b_z = -3\) and none of them from \(b_z = +3\), which would give \(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = +5\) instead. The stem is transcribed as printed; work the example with \(-3\hat{k}\).] \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b} = (3\hat{i} - 4\hat{j} + 5\hat{k})\cdot(-2\hat{i} + \hat{j} - 3\hat{k})\)

\(= -6 - 4 - 15\)

\(= -25\)

\(\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 3 & -4 & 5 \\ -2 & 1 & -3 \end{vmatrix} = 7\hat{i} - \hat{j} - 5\hat{k}\)

Note \(\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{a} = -7\hat{i} + \hat{j} + 5\hat{k}\)
_note: PRINTED DEFECT (stem contradicts its own solution). The stem prints the third component of b as +3k, but every step of the book's printed solution uses -3k: the dot product is written out as (-2i + j - 3k), the determinant's third row is printed as (-2, 1, -3), and both printed results require it. Verified at 6x magnification on the rendered page. Checks: with b_z = -3, a.b = -6 - 4 - 15 = -25 (as printed) and a x b = 7i - j - 5k (as printed); with the stem's b_z = +3, a.b = +5 and a x b = -17i - 19j - 5k, matching NEITHER printed result. The book's third printed result, b x a = -7i + j + 5k, also requires b_z = -3. The stem's sign is the outlier, so the printed +3k is the misprint. Transcribed faithfully as printed.

stem: Find the torque of a force \(7\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} - 5\hat{k}\) about the origin. The force acts on a particle whose position vector is \(\hat{i} - \hat{j} + \hat{k}\).
solution:
Here \(\mathbf{r} = \hat{i} - \hat{j} + \hat{k}\) and \(\mathbf{F} = 7\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} - 5\hat{k}\).

We shall use the determinant rule to find the torque \(\boldsymbol{\tau} = \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{F}\)

\(\boldsymbol{\tau} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 1 & -1 & 1 \\ 7 & 3 & -5 \end{vmatrix} = (5 - 3)\hat{i} - (-5 - 7)\hat{j} + (3 - (-7))\hat{k}\)

or \(\boldsymbol{\tau} = 2\hat{i} + 12\hat{j} + 10\hat{k}\)

stem: Show that the angular momentum about any point of a single particle moving with constant velocity remains constant throughout the motion.
solution:
Let the particle with velocity \(\mathbf{v}\) be at point P at some instant \(t\). We want to calculate the angular momentum of the particle about an arbitrary point O.

The angular momentum is \(\mathbf{l} = \mathbf{r} \times m\mathbf{v}\). Its magnitude is \(mvr\sin\theta\), where \(\theta\) is the angle between \(\mathbf{r}\) and \(\mathbf{v}\) as shown in Fig. 6.19. Although the particle changes position with time, the line of direction of \(\mathbf{v}\) remains the same and hence \(OM = r\sin\theta\) is a constant.

Further, the direction of \(\mathbf{l}\) is perpendicular to the plane of \(\mathbf{r}\) and \(\mathbf{v}\). It is into the page of the figure. This direction does not change with time.

Thus, \(\mathbf{l}\) remains the same in magnitude and direction and is therefore conserved. Is there any external torque on the particle?
